prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not give ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or any other cephalosporin: documented cephalosporin allergy with urticaria.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Give meropenem 2 g IV every 8 hours with vancomycin within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for lumbar puncture, withholding ceftriaxone for the documented cephalosporin urticaria (meropenem also covers Listeria); narrow to the isolate's susceptibilities.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 12, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose with paired blood glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) or ampicillin IV for Streptococcus pneumoniae with penicillin MIC 0.06 mg/L (susceptible by CLSI meningitis breakpoints).
ENT assessment for drainage of the maxillary and ethmoid sinus source.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

differential.key_features: Excluded: neutrophilic CSF (3414 cells/microL, 94% neutrophils), glucose ratio 0.06, Gram-positive diplococci and S. pneumoniae on PCR; enterovirus, HSV and VZV not detected.
No seizures or focal deficits; HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected on the CSF panel; pyogenic CSF with a bacterial isolate.

differential.diagnosis: Subdural empyema or brain abscess complicating sinusitis
differential.key_features: Sinus source makes it a complication to look for; no focal signs or seizures, and CT shows no collection or focal lesion and no bony erosion. Contrast MRI if focal signs appear or the patient fails to improve.
Excluded: 12-hour course, neutrophilic CSF and S. pneumoniae identified, against a subacute lymphocytic picture.
Immunocompetent host, HIV non-reactive, Cryptococcus not detected on the CSF panel.
Gradual headache with fever, no hemorrhage on CT, turbid neutrophilic CSF.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 12, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

With an immediate-type cephalosporin allergy (urticaria), meropenem with vancomycin replaces ceftriaxone; therapy is narrowed to benzylpenicillin or ampicillin once the isolate is penicillin-susceptible (MIC 0.06 mg/L or less by CLSI meningitis breakpoints).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild hyponatraemia is common in acute bacterial meningitis (inappropriate ADH secretion, or volume depletion from vomiting and fever, as the raised urea suggests); it is a complication of the illness, not an alternative explanation. Assess volume status before any fluid restriction.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Parameningeal sinus disease is the likely SOURCE of the pneumococcal meningitis, not an alternative diagnosis; the CSF profile remains the deciding evidence.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest uncomplicated sinusitis as the source of headache and fever, deferring meningitis evaluation.

sequence_constraints.reason: Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

clinical_pearls: The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status is present in only about 44% of bacterial meningitis cases, but at least two of the four symptoms (headache, fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status) are present in 95%
Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults, followed by Neisseria meningitidis
Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis from approximately 34% to 14% when given before or with the first dose of antibiotics
A CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 has a sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 98% for bacterial meningitis

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Washington is a 45-year-old right-handed IT project manager who also coaches high school basketball and was brought to the emergency department by his wife at approximately 06:15 this morning. His wife reports that he came home from practice yesterday afternoon complaining of a progressively worsening headache that he initially attributed to a sinus flare-up, given his chronic sinusitis history. He took 800 mg of ibuprofen and went to bed early at around 20:00. She checked on him at 23:00 and noted he felt warm to the touch and was sweating profusely. She took his temperature with a home thermometer and recorded 38.9 degrees Celsius. She gave him 1000 mg of acetaminophen and encouraged fluids. Overnight, he became progressively more confused and agitated, calling out names she did not recognize and not responding appropriately to her questions. By 05:30 this morning, she found him curled in the fetal position in bed, moaning, with his hands covering his eyes. He complained that the bedroom light was unbearable and that his neck felt stiff and painful. He vomited twice. He was unable to stand without assistance. On arrival to the ED, his temperature was 39.5 degrees Celsius. He was tachycardic and appeared acutely ill, diaphoretic, and photophobic. He could state his name but was unable to provide any further history. His wife denies any recent travel, sick contacts with meningitis, or known immunocompromised state, though she notes he has been more tired than usual over the past week and had nasal congestion he attributed to allergies. She confirms his vaccinations are up to date for his age but is unsure about meningococcal vaccination. There is no history of head trauma, seizure activity, or new rash.
